readerTitle: The meeting where nobody said no
caseNote: 가상 사례 (난방·배관 서비스 회사, B2B 마케팅 에이전시) · 적용 레슨, 새 개념 없음
insight: 만장일치가 빠를수록, 특히 윗사람이 먼저 말했을 때는, 그 침묵이 동의인지 눈치인지를 먼저 의심한다.
misconception: 회의에서 아무도 반대하지 않았다면 모두가 동의한 것이고, '우려 있으면 말해 달라'고 물으면 충분하다.

sources.text: Janis, I. L. (1972). Victims of Groupthink. Houghton Mifflin. (집단사고 개념의 배경)
모든 사례와 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(Maria의 배관 회사, 에이전시 피치 리뷰)와 인용은 설명용 가상입니다. 실제 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
권위 편향·집단사고 설명이 THK-03-01, THK-03-02 개념 레슨의 정의와 표현이 일치하는지 게시 전에 맞춰 보세요.
'리더가 마지막에 말하기', '토론 전 개인별 서면 의견 받기'는 일반적인 회의 운영 권고로 제시했습니다. 특정 연구 결과로 표현하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The meeting took eleven minutes.
body: Maria runs a heating and plumbing company with eight staff. She opens the Monday meeting: "I want to launch a yearly service plan. One price, all repair visits included. I think it's our future."
Three nods. One "sounds great." Nobody else speaks. The decision is made by 9:11.

image.label: A small team nodding around a table while one person speaks
image.brief: 작은 사무실 회의 테이블. 사장이 서서 말하고, 직원 여섯 명이 고개를 끄덕이지만 두 명은 시선을 피하고 손에 든 메모를 덮고 있음. 벽시계는 9:11. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: You're Maria's operations manager.
body: The vote was unanimous. Maria asks you to start building the plan this week.

options.text: Start building. Eight people agreed, and they know the work.
options.feedback: You gain speed, but you're counting silence as a yes. When the boss speaks first and nobody pushes back, the agreement may be with Maria, not with the plan. That's **authority bias** at work.

options.text: Send a group message asking if anyone has concerns.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but a group chat is still a public room. People who stayed quiet in the meeting rarely object in front of the same audience. The pull toward harmony, **groupthink**, follows them.

options.text: Ask each person privately to write the one thing most likely to go wrong.
options.feedback: Private, specific and expected, so disagreeing costs nothing socially. You lose a day and may hear things Maria won't enjoy.

cards.title: The quiet people knew something.
body: The notes came back the next day. Two senior technicians raised the same point: in a cold January, emergency calls pile up. Under "all visits included", every one of them would be free.
The office manager added that the keenest sign-ups would likely be owners of the oldest, least reliable boilers.
None of this came up at 9:05. Asked why, one technician said: "Maria had already called it our future. Who argues with that?"

cards.title: Two forces, one silent room.
body: **Authority bias:** we give extra weight to the most senior person's view and hesitate to contradict it. Maria spoke first and called the plan "our future", so any doubt now meant disagreeing with the boss.
**Groupthink:** a close team values harmony, so doubts stay unspoken, and each person reads the others' silence as real agreement.
Together they produce a meeting that looks unanimous and isn't.

image.label: Speech bubbles: one large from the boss, small empty ones from the team
image.brief: 회의 장면을 위에서 본 인포그래픽. 사장 쪽에 큰 말풍선 "Our future", 나머지 사람들 머리 위에는 작은 말풍선 안에 "?"나 "Winter calls..." 같은 생각이 희미하게 보이지만 입은 닫혀 있음. 왼쪽 라벨 "Authority bias", 오른쪽 라벨 "Groupthink".

cards.title: Polite agreement has a pattern.
body: Watch for these signs in any decision meeting:
list: A fast yes on a big, hard-to-reverse decision
The most senior person spoke first and framed the answer
No one named a risk, a cost or an alternative
The people closest to the work said the least
cards.callout: See two or more? Collect views privately before the decision is final.

cards.title: Not every quick yes is a problem.
body: Sometimes a team agrees because the idea is good and obvious. Running private surveys on every small choice slows everyone down and tells people their yes isn't trusted. Save the extra step for decisions that are expensive or hard to undo.
And asking for doubts only works if doubts change something. If Maria hears the boiler point and launches unchanged without a word, next time the notes will come back blank.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: You run a pitch review at a 30-person B2B agency. The founder opens: "This is our strongest pitch. The client will love it."
The account manager, who talks to this client every week, is staring at her laptop. The pitch is Thursday. How do you run the next 20 minutes?

options.text: Turn to the account manager: "You know them best. Do you agree?"
options.feedback: Right person, wrong question. A yes-or-no question asked right after the founder's verdict makes "yes" the easy answer. **Authority bias** is still in the room.

options.text: Ask everyone for one reason the client might say no, most junior first, founder last.
options.feedback: Doubt becomes the task, not a challenge to the founder. Junior-first order weakens **authority bias**, and asking everyone breaks the **groupthink** silence. It costs the founder a little comfort.

options.text: Appoint one person as devil's advocate to attack the pitch.
options.feedback: It gives doubt a seat, but everyone knows it's a role. The account manager's real concern can still go unsaid while someone else plays the part.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams see this in roadmap reviews. The founder demos a favorite feature, and engineers who know it will take three months stay quiet. Collect written estimates and risks before the demo, not after.

cards.title: A silent room isn't a yes.
body: Concepts used: **authority bias**, when the boss speaks first and others defer; **groupthink**, when harmony keeps doubts unspoken.
**Try it today:** in your next decision meeting, speak last. Before any discussion, ask each person to write down one risk.
